title: HKMA self-assessment overdue, STR quality findings still open across Hong Kong AIs
summary: No breaking enforcement today, so Alex and Jordan go deep on two live HKMA obligations: the annual AML/CFT self-assessment return and the still-open Q4 2025 STR quality thematic findings. Plus a read on cross-boundary risk as Huanggang Port reopens.
script:
ALEX: There is a pattern in today's digest that I think is more urgent than it looks at first glance. We have two Hong Kong obligations sitting on the board simultaneously, one of them overdue and marked high priority, and a structural change to cross-boundary movement that lands this week. None of it is a single headline. But together it adds up to a genuinely uncomfortable week to be an MLRO at an HKMA-supervised institution. This is AML Agents Briefing for Monday the twelfth of October.

JORDAN: I want to get into all of that. But I'd push back slightly on the framing. You said "simultaneously," and that's technically true. The annual AML/CFT self-assessment return under HKMA's AML/CFT Guideline section 11 was due on the thirtieth of September. That date has passed. And the STR quality thematic review closure from the Q4 2025 cycle is also overdue, flagged high priority. So we're not talking about two things approaching. We're talking about two things that should already be done.

ALEX: Fair. Let's take the self-assessment first because it's the one with the broader scope. This is the annual return to the HKMA covering eight discrete areas: customer due diligence, ongoing monitoring, sanctions screening, suspicious transaction reporting, training, governance, and independent audit. If you're an authorised institution and your return hasn't landed with HKMA yet, the question is not whether you are late. The question is how late, and whether you've communicated proactively with your supervisory team.

JORDAN: And here's where I'd actually defend the MLRO in this situation, which you might not expect from me. The self-assessment is genuinely hard to complete well. It is not a tick-box exercise, or at least it shouldn't be. Getting honest, board-approved attestations across all eight areas requires inputs from legal, from risk, from operations, sometimes from group functions sitting outside Hong Kong. If you're a branch of a global bank, your independence of audit evidence might sit in a different time zone.

ALEX: That's all true. But the deadline isn't new. It's the same date every year. The HKMA's expectation is that institutions are not starting this process in late September.

JORDAN: No, and I agree with that. The point I'd make to any MLRO listening is: if your return is late, file it now and accompany it with a cover note explaining the delay. Don't wait until your supervisor asks. The HKMA's communication pattern in examinations consistently distinguishes between institutions that self-identify process gaps and those that wait to be found. That distinction matters when findings are being graded.

ALEX: That's the right read. Now the STR quality thematic. This one concerns me more, operationally, because it's not about governance paperwork. The HKMA ran a Q4 2025 thematic review of suspicious transaction report narrative quality across the supervised population. Deficiency letters went to roughly twenty-five percent of authorised institutions in early 2026. Closure of those findings is the current obligation, and it's marked overdue.

JORDAN: And I want to push on that "twenty-five percent" figure. That is one in four supervised banks receiving a deficiency letter on STR narrative quality. That is not a tail-risk number. That is a systemic signal. Which tells me the HKMA is not satisfied with how institutions are describing the basis for suspicion, the typology, the customer context. The question for an MLRO who received that letter is not "have we acknowledged the finding?" It's "have we actually changed how our analysts write STR narratives?"

ALEX: I'd add a supervisory read to that. When a regulator runs a thematic and finds deficiencies in twenty-five percent of the population, the follow-up is rarely a one-and-done exercise. The HKMA has form for returning to thematic subjects in subsequent examination cycles. If your institution received a deficiency letter and you've closed it procedurally without substantive change, that closure may not hold under scrutiny.

JORDAN: So what should listeners do this week? First, if you're the MLRO at an HKMA-supervised institution and your annual self-assessment return has not been filed, file it today and send a proactive note to your supervisory contact. Do not wait to be chased. Second, if your institution received a deficiency letter from the Q4 2025 STR quality thematic, pull three recent STR narratives and apply the HKMA's own quality criteria against them. If you cannot clearly identify the element of suspicion, the customer behaviour pattern, and the AML/CFT typology in each narrative, your remediation is incomplete.

ALEX: And document that internal review. Put it on paper. If an examiner comes back around on this subject, you want to be able to show a dated, documented quality-assurance exercise, not just a process update in the procedure manual.

JORDAN: Agreed. Moving on, and I want to spend a moment on the Huanggang Port reopening. The revamped checkpoint between Hong Kong and Shenzhen opens on the thirteenth of October, operating twenty-four hours. The framing in the public commentary is connectivity and Greater Bay Area integration. That framing is not wrong. But it is not complete.

ALEX: From a supervisory angle, this is a structural change to cross-boundary movement volume and pattern. Any change to the physical and financial flows between Hong Kong and the mainland is a risk-environment change. Not a red flag in itself, but a prompt to review your geographic risk assessments.

JORDAN: And I'd be more specific. For trade finance teams at Hong Kong banks, increased cross-boundary logistics creates additional surface area for trade-based money laundering. For private banks and wealth managers serving Greater Bay Area clients, increased movement of individuals is worth noting in your customer risk segmentation. The question is not whether this changes your risk appetite. It's whether your risk assessment documentation reflects the current operating environment, not the one from two years ago.

ALEX: That's the point. A risk assessment that predates a significant structural change in the geography it covers is, by definition, out of date.

JORDAN: Exactly. Before we close, a word on the APEC Finance Ministers' Meeting, which Hong Kong is hosting later this month. Financial Secretary Paul Chan has flagged digital infrastructure financing and inclusive finance as two of the four priority themes. Neither of those is directly an AML story. But multilateral finance convenings of this type consistently precede new commitments on information sharing and beneficial ownership transparency. Worth watching for any communique language that signals regulatory movement in those areas.

ALEX: And we'll cover it here if anything material comes out of it. That's the week set up. The full obligation register, source links, and today's digest are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app.

JORDAN: If those two Hong Kong deadlines felt uncomfortably close to home, that's the point. Get the self-assessment filed. Pull those STR narratives. Don't wait for the examiner to ask. See you tomorrow.
